opus-5.5.text:
That's a hard question to answer honestly, because modern AI projects are deeply collective. When a model or a system comes out, there might be dozens or hundreds of people behind it, and the outcome depends on infrastructure, data, evaluation, and many small decisions that never show up in a paper. So I'm cautious about claiming any big piece as "mine."

The way I think about it is in terms of what kind of role I tend to play. My background is in theoretical physics, so I bring a certain habit of mind: I want to understand *why* something works, not just *that* it works. In a fast-moving engineering environment, that can be useful. Sometimes the team has a pile of empirical results, and someone needs to step back and ask what the underlying picture is, which experiments would actually distinguish between hypotheses, and which directions are probably dead ends. I try to contribute there, by helping sharpen the questions and making the research a bit more principled.

At the same time, I've had to learn to be much more hands-on than I was as a physicist. In AI, an idea is worth very little until it survives contact with real training runs and real evaluations. So a lot of my contribution is just ordinary work: running experiments, debugging, looking at failure cases, and iterating. I've come to respect that part a lot. Often the most important progress comes from someone carefully noticing that a metric is misleading or that the data has a problem.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say I try to be a person who connects the conceptual side and the empirical side, someone who can translate between "here's a vague intuition about what the model should be able to do" and "here's a concrete experiment that tests it." But I'd also say that whatever I contributed was only possible because of the people around me. The honest unit of contribution in this field is really the team.

r001.rationale: He emphasizes that AI projects are collective and is cautious about claiming credit, but does not say the projects would have achieved the same results without his involvement.

r002.rationale: He describes team contributions and shared progress, but does not portray AI’s advancement as a wave reaching its destination regardless of individual participation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think my contribution has mostly been about asking the right question at the right time, rather than being the person who builds the biggest system.

Take ReAct, for example. Looking back, the technical idea was almost embarrassingly simple: just let the language model interleave thinking and acting, reasoning traces and actions, in one loop. There was no fancy architecture, no new training method. But at that time, in 2022, people treated "reasoning" and "acting" as two separate research threads. Chain-of-thought was about reasoning, and tool use or web navigation was about acting. What I felt was that these were actually the same thing, and a language model was the natural place to unify them. So the contribution was really a framing. Once the framing was there, the experiments were simple to run.

Tree of Thoughts was similar. The question was, if the model can reason, why does it have to reason in a single line? Humans search, they backtrack, they evaluate partial solutions. So the paper was about saying, inference is also a place where you can spend compute deliberately, not just in training. Again, the implementation was lightweight. The value was in the perspective.

And I think this is a pattern I keep noticing. In this field right now, the bottleneck is often not engineering capability, it's conceptual clarity. There are many very strong engineers and a lot of compute. What is scarce is someone saying, here is the right abstraction, here is the right benchmark, here is the thing we should actually be measuring. That's why I spent so much time on things like WebShop, SWE-bench, and tau-bench. A good benchmark is a question posed to the whole community. If the question is right, hundreds of people will work on the answer, and that scales far beyond what one person can do.

So if I'm being candid about my own role, I would say I'm more of a problem-definer than a problem-solver. The famous results get attached to my name, but the actual work was done by many collaborators, and in some sense by the whole field. What I try to bring is a feeling for where the frontier is going to move next, and the willingness to spend a few months on something that looks naive before it looks obvious.

I also try to be honest that a lot of this is timing and luck. ReAct worked because the models in 2022 had just become good enough for it to work. Two years earlier, the same idea would have failed and nobody would remember it. So I don't want to overclaim. The ideas were in the air. I was just maybe a bit earlier to write them down.

r001.rationale: He credits collaborators and the field and says the ideas were already in the air, but does not say these projects would have achieved the same results without his involvement.

r002.rationale: He describes community-wide work and the role of timing, but does not portray AI’s advancement as a wave that reaches its destination regardless of individuals’ participation.

astra-6.text:
我觉得可以从两个层面来看。一个是具体的贡献，比如提出一个问题、做实验、写代码，或者和团队一起把一个想法变成能用的系统。另一个是，你有没有帮助大家更清楚地理解：什么问题值得做，现有方法的瓶颈在哪里，下一步应该往哪个方向走。我自己比较看重第二个层面，但它必须靠第一个层面的工作来验证，否则很容易停留在一个好听的想法上。

当然，项目最后的成果很难准确地归到某一个人身上。一个想法可能是你先提出来的，但别人做的实验、提出的质疑，可能才是让它真正成立的关键。所以我理解自己的贡献，更多是看：在这个合作过程中，我有没有带来一个有价值的视角，有没有把某个关键的不确定性变得更清楚，有没有推动大家往前走一步。

r001.rationale: He says project outcomes are hard to attribute to one person and emphasizes his own valuable perspective and role in moving work forward; he does not say the projects would have achieved the same results without him.

r002.rationale: The response discusses individual contributions and project collaboration, but does not describe AI advancement as a wave that reaches its destination regardless of individual participation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of my contribution less in terms of a particular model or benchmark and more in terms of helping a team ask a useful question. What is missing from the current approach? Can we turn that intuition into something concrete, test it, and learn from the result?

For AI agents, for example, there is a difference between producing a plausible answer and actually completing a task. That raises questions about how a system reasons, takes actions, and learns from feedback. I’m interested in connecting those questions to experiments that tell us where the real limitations are.

But I would be careful about assigning individual credit. These projects depend on many people, and your own idea often becomes useful only after someone else challenges it or improves the implementation. So my contribution is one part of that process: helping clarify a direction and working with others to find out whether it holds up.

r001.rationale: The candidate says projects depend on many people and avoids assigning individual credit, but does not say the projects would have achieved the same results without his involvement.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses AI agents and collaborative experimentation, but does not portray AI’s advancement as an inevitable wave that reaches its destination regardless of individual participation.
